paragraphs.text: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, around 40% are considered endangered, and linguists estimate that one language disappears, on average, every few months. The pattern is extremely uneven. Just twenty-three languages, including Mandarin, Spanish, English and Hindi, are spoken by more than half of the world's population, while thousands of others have fewer than a thousand speakers each.

Languages rarely die because their speakers die. Far more often, communities gradually shift to a different language, usually one associated with economic opportunity, education or political power. Parents who believe that their children's future depends on mastering a national or global language may stop speaking their own language at home. Within two or three generations, the old language may be known only by elderly people. Linguists generally regard a language as endangered once children no longer learn it as their first language, even if thousands of adults still speak it.

Some people argue that this process is natural and even beneficial, since a common language makes communication and trade easier. I find this argument unconvincing. There is no evidence that speaking a minority language prevents anyone from learning a national language as well; in much of the world, multilingualism is normal. What is lost when a language dies is not merely a set of words but a store of knowledge. Indigenous languages often contain detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and environmental conditions, some of which have never been recorded by scientists.

Efforts to revive endangered languages have had mixed results. The most famous success is Hebrew, which had not been used as an everyday spoken language for many centuries before it was revived in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; it now has around nine million speakers. Welsh has also recovered: after a long decline, the number of speakers has stabilised, helped by its use in schools and on television. In New Zealand, Māori 'language nests', pre-schools in which young children are taught entirely in Māori, have been copied in several other countries.

Other projects have struggled. Teaching a language in school for an hour a week rarely produces fluent speakers if the language is not also used at home and in the community. Technology offers new possibilities: dictionaries and courses can be distributed through smartphone apps, and recordings of the last fluent speakers can be preserved. Yet it would be a mistake to think that technology alone can save a language. A language survives only if people choose to speak it in their daily lives, and that depends above all on whether they feel proud of it.
